sermon.title: Grace Notes
sermon.speaker: Pastor David G. Kincer
sermon.summary: In this message Pastor David G. Kincer begins in 1 Corinthians 15 with the gospel and the evidence for the resurrection, then teaches that grace is not only a favor but a power, “the divine influence upon the heart,” that moved Paul to work. He follows grace through John 1, Luke 2, Luke 6, Acts 11 and Colossians 3, and asks whether our grace is increasing.
sermon.transcript_source: This transcript comes from YouTube’s automatic English captions, which supply the timing and the words. Punctuation, capitalization and paragraphing were added by hand, and obvious caption errors were corrected; his wording was not rewritten. “[unclear]” marks a word or name that was not clear. Editor note: the captions garble a few words; three spots are shown as [unclear] and not guessed: a name in 1 Corinthians 15:5 at about 4:15, a name for a neighbor at about 15:00, and a word for the group of Greek-speaking people in Acts 11 at about 17:26. In the captions “lawn more,” “wheat eater,” and “part ful” are shown as “lawn mower,” “weed eater,” and “powerful.” He says the two disciples talking with Jesus in Luke 24 were “on the road to Damascus”; that account is on the road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13), and the NKJV text shown is Luke 24:13-21. He also says that Jesus went “down into, uh, where the dead souls were and preached to them before the flood” and that Judas saw Him there; these are his own statements and are not part of the passage he is reading. He says “Luke 6:32” and explains the word “thank” as grace; the NKJV text of Luke 6:32 reads “what credit is that to you?” He mentions a neighbor and a “Mr. Barnes” as examples, in the transcript only. “[Unclear]” marks three spots.

chunks.section_question: What responses to the gospel does Paul describe? (1 Corinthians 15:1-2)
chunks.short_answer: Reading 1 Corinthians 15:1-2, he says there are two choices: “you can reject it or you can accept it.” He says “Receive means you accept it, you take it,” to stand means “you take your stand, you continue in it, you don’t waver,” and being saved means “you’re rescued, you’re set free from sin, from hell, from the lake of fire, and from the day of wrath.”
chunks.text:
We are in chapter 15, and in chapter 15, verse 1, Paul says, “I declare to you the gospel which I preached.” Now, there are four responses here to when he preached the gospel, and this is what the gospel should do. “Which you have received.” You accept it. See, you got two choices: you can reject it or you can accept it. Receive means you accept it, you take it. All right. Number two, “in which you stand.” You see, you take your stand, you continue in it, you don’t waver.

Number three, “by which also you are saved.” You’re rescued, you’re set free from sin, from hell, from the lake of fire, and from the day of wrath.

For instance, if God judged America in His anger to correct them, you would be rescued from that wrath of God, and then there’s a day of wrath coming at the end.

chunks.short_answer: He says to hold fast means “we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit,” because “if you let it go, it doesn’t do you any good.” He says the gospel is that “Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures,” which means the Old and New Testaments are both Scripture, and he says “the Old Testament is still for today.”
chunks.text: Then He says, “if you hold fast.” See, we also hold fast, we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit, to what was preached, this gospel that was preached, “unless you believed in vain,” or your belief was worthless. If you let it go, it doesn’t do you any good. And then he is going to tell us what the gospel is. He said, “For I delivered unto you first of all that which also I received: how that, number one, Christ died for our sins according to the Scriptures.” Now, that means the Old Testament is considered Scriptures, and the New Testament is considered Scriptures, because the Gospels and the epistles talk about the death and burial and resurrection of Christ. chunks.section_question: What does “full of grace and truth” mean, and what did grace do for Peter? (John 1:14, 1:17)
chunks.short_answer: He reads that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” and was full of grace and truth, so receiving Christ means “receiving what? Grace and truth.” He says the disciples went back to fishing, and “Grace came after them.” Although the Bible says “If you deny me, I will deny you before my Father,” he says “grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back.”
chunks.text:
Now, you know more about the Bible definition when you see its use in the Scripture. All right, now watch this. “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us,” which is Jesus. We all know that, right? Jesus was the Word, Jesus was God, He became flesh, dwelt among us, and He was full of what? Grace and truth. So when I receive Christ in my life, I’m receiving what? Grace and truth. Hallelujah. And we can, we can back that up. When Jesus told them, “I got to go away, I will come again,” so he died and he what? Rose and came back to them. See, that’s truth. He told him the truth. Right?

But you know, Peter denied Him, Peter cursed first. Uh, Peter challenged Him, and then Peter got all the disciples to go back to work. They went back to fishing after He rose from the grave. And what did grace do? Grace came after them. See, Jesus came after them. See, Jesus is filled with grace. See, He’s going to do everything He can to get you to reach the maturity and the completeness of His goals and His promises. Ain’t that beautiful? See, He kept His word, He spoke the truth, and then what He didn’t, He put aside the fact that Peter denied Him, and the Bible says, “If you deny me, I will deny you before my Father,” yet grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back.

And, folks, if, if Peter can do something that cannot be forgiven, how much more will God reach out to us in our failures and in our, uh, amen. So grace is important. Truth’s also important. Hallelujah. Now, “the law was given through Moses,” in John 1:17, “but grace and truth came through Jesus Christ.” All right, that divine influence came through Jesus Christ.

Now Luke 2:40, speaking of Jesus when he’s like 12 years old, the grace of God was what? Upon Him. Now, He was what? Filled with grace, but in His human form He was. He increased in grace, look at this, “with God and men.” You see, grace moved Him to please the Father.

chunks.section_question: How does he say grace is different from a favor? (Luke 6:32)
chunks.short_answer: He says doing a neighbor favors or giving him money “doesn’t change him,” but “if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about.” He says “God’s just not out to do us favors, folks. He’s out to make us in His likeness and His image.” From Luke 6:32 he says “the word thank is the what word? Grace,” and that grace is a “power by God to treat people better than they’re treating you.”
chunks.text:
And so grace is that power that moves us. Now, we’re not talking about the baptism of the Holy Ghost, we’re talking about grace. Grace isn’t some, you know, “the favor of God was upon him.” You know, I can do Mr. [unclear] here a favor. He lives close to me. I lend him a lawn mower. Not a lawnmower, he’s got a better one than I do. I lend him my weed eater, and I lend him this, and I lend him that. That doesn’t change him, that doesn’t make his character any better than it was before I’m doing. I could give him $1,000 dollars, and it’s not going to change his character. I did him a favor. Are you there? But if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about. Hallelujah.

See, God’s just not out to do us favors, folks. He’s out to make us in His likeness and His image, make, make us a light to the world where people can see God in us. How many could use a little increase in grace? Yeah. You know, if Jesus increased in grace, who was full of grace, how many know we should strive to increase in grace, this grace that moves us to please God and to help people? chunks.section_question: What did Barnabas see at Antioch? (Acts 11:23)
chunks.short_answer: He says grace is not something to “just take it as this favor word”: “He more than favors you, He is empowering you to please Him and to help others in this life.” In Acts 11:23 he says Barnabas “had seen the grace of God” because the Greeks were “now serving God and repenting from their sins and turning to what’s right.” He says grace “is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it,” and that “He’s going to keep after you.”
chunks.text:
I submit to you this morning, grace is a very powerful thing, and we shouldn’t just take it lightly, and we shouldn’t just take it as this favor word. “No matter what, or do God favors me.” No, He more than favors you, He is empowering you to please Him and to help others in this life. Now, Acts 11:23, Barnabas went down to Antioch. They had preached Christ to the [unclear], the Greeks, the Greek cultured people, and many of these Greeks believed it. It said before that they had only been preaching to Jews only, but here it says at Antioch they preached to the Greeks, see, the non-Jews, the Greek-speaking people, culture. And so when Barnabas came and had seen, see that word, he had seen the grace of God. Remember, the definition was reflection in life. See, he saw the grace of God. Why? Because he saw these Greeks now serving God and repenting from their sins and turning to what’s right. He saw the grace of God in evidence in the Greeks. Isn’t that powerful?

The grace is a very powerful thing, and too many people just got this favor thing, and they don’t understand the power that’s in the grace of God, and it’s a free gift that He gives us. Grace, the Bible says, is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it. See, Mr. Barnes could lend me his lawnmower, but if I never used it to mow my lawn, it what? Doesn’t do any good. Hallelujah. Now, “and he was glad, and encouraged them all with purpose of heart to continue with the Lord.” See, they had turned to the Lord. Isn’t that powerful? Should grace be seen in our life? Yes, church.

Not only will Jesus go to the extreme to influence you to live for Him, I don’t care if you’re committing adultery, drunkenness, He’s going to keep after you. Why? ‘Cause He’s full of grace, and He wants to win you back, He wants to improve your life. But grace also is a power that works in me, that works in you, to help people and live a life that’s pleasing to God. Now, that changes everything.

chunks.section_question: How does grace relate to worship and the word? (Colossians 3:16, Acts 20:32)
chunks.short_answer: Reading Colossians 3:16, he says singing “with grace in your hearts” means singing with “the divine influence of God.” He says “Grace wants you to worship God. Why? Because it’s a principle of God that brings His presence. When His presence comes, you start taking on His nature.” Reading Acts 20:32, he says the Scriptures are “grace, that divine influence upon your mind, your emotions, and your will.”
chunks.text:
Colossians 3:16, “Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.” Singing with favor, singing with benefits, or singing with the divine influence of God upon you. Amen. See, and it agrees with the Holy Spirit. See, the Holy Spirit came upon them, the Holy Spirit was with them, and they did things by the Spirit. Here, grace comes upon, grace is with us, grace is working in us, and it’s the same result. We want to worship God. People that don’t want to worship God, they need an increase of grace. Yeah. Grace wants you to worship God. Why? Because it’s a principle of God that brings His presence. When His presence comes, you start taking on His nature. Hallelujah. Powerful, very powerful.

Now, Acts 20:32, “I commend you to God, and I commend you to the word of grace.” Oh, see, the Scriptures are what? Grace, that divine influence upon your mind, your emotions, and your will to make you into someone who can act different than the people of the world. Isn’t that beautiful? And again, we’re not talking about the baptism of the Holy Ghost, we’re talking about grace. So even if you reject the infilling of the Holy Ghost, there’s still power in what? Grace. Power. Now, what does this grace do? Grace is able to what? Build you up. Build you up to what? His likeness and His image. He’s out to make you a light to the world, that people can see your good works and bring glory and honor to Jesus Christ. Isn’t that beautiful? Hallelujah. See, grace not only worked in Paul, drove him to work, but grace built Paul up to be the apostle that God had intended him to be.

chunks.section_question: Can everyone be a light to the world, and what inheritance does grace give?
chunks.short_answer: He says “you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ.” He says someone who stays a drunkard after being saved would show no “reflection” of grace, but at Antioch “he saw the change in their life.” He says grace “will give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified,” and that Jesus “has activated the will” through His death and resurrection.
chunks.text:
Now, you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ. Can’t we all be disciples? Can we all come to maturity? Yes. We may not be a prophet, we may not be an apostle, we may not be a pastor, but we can be a light to the world. We can be a disciple of Christ that people can see the results of grace in. See, if I’m a drunkard and I get saved and I stay a drunkard, when Barnabas come, he would not have what? Seen the grace of God. Why? ‘Cause there’s no reflection. See, but there was a reflection when he went down there to Antioch. He saw the change in their life. And, folks, that’s what grace will do to all of us.

And this grace will give you an inheritance among all them which are sanctified.

Now, we have an inheritance: Jesus Christ, the gifts of the Spirit, the fruit of the Spirit, the wisdom and knowledge, understanding and counsel and strength, and all these things are part of our inheritance. And he says grace is able to give you, to obtain this inheritance that God has promised, because Jesus, Jesus died on the cross. There cannot be an inheritance without the death of the one who wrote the will, and he’s dead, folks. And he come back to alive, and so we, he has activated the will, and we can have our inheritance if we will embrace grace and let grace work in our life.

chunks.section_question: Are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited?
chunks.short_answer: He says some Christians “just take favor, go to heaven, wait for the rapture,” while others “grow in grace” and so have more influence in “changing people’s lives and bringing them to Christ.” He asks, “are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited?” and says grace “will change that and put a focus on Jesus and his focus on others.”
chunks.text: See, why is it that some Christians are concerned about others, are concerned about, about going to church, and are concerned about growing? They’ve entered into a dimension of grace. See, that’s influencing them. Others, they just take favor, go to heaven, wait for the rapture, that’s it. They do what they want, they stay home, they don’t pray, they don’t, you know, they can’t win souls to Christ because they don’t know the word or anything else. But others, they respond to that grace, and they grow in grace, and the more they grow, the more influence they have in helping people and changing people’s lives and bringing them to Christ. My question, or the, I should say the Holy Spirit’s question to us this morning is: are you increasing in grace, or is your grace limited? If you don’t like things or you, you don’t want to do things, you just don’t do them. You got no influence of God to overcome your personal desires and wishes and laziness and attitude and beliefs. Everything’s got to be for you and focused on you. Grace will change that and put a focus on Jesus and his focus on others to come to him and grow in him.

faqs.question: What does he say “receive” means?
faqs.answer: He says “Receive means you accept it, you take it.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Moreover, brethren, I declare to you the gospel which I preached to you, which also you received and in which you stand, by which also you are saved, if you hold fast that word which I preached to you—unless you believed in vain.

faqs.question: What does he say it means to hold fast to the gospel?
faqs.answer: He says “we hang on, we don’t give up, we don’t quit,” and that if you let it go, “it doesn’t do you any good.”

faqs.question: Does he say the Old Testament is still for today?
faqs.answer: Yes. He says some churches say it is not, but “the Old Testament is still for today.”

faqs.question: Which days does he count for the burial and resurrection?
faqs.answer: He says Jesus died on Friday, was in the grave on Saturday, and arose on Sunday, and he calls trying “to keep Jesus in the grave for three 24-hour periods” ridiculous.

scriptures.text_nkjv: and that He was buried, and that He rose again the third day according to the Scriptures,

faqs.question: How many people does he say saw Jesus after the resurrection?
faqs.answer: He says “there’s over 500 people that witnessed Jesus alive and well on planet Earth after he died.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: and that He was seen by Cephas, then by the twelve. After that He was seen by over five hundred brethren at once, of whom the greater part remain to the present, but some have fallen asleep. After that He was seen by James, then by all the apostles. Then last of all He was seen by me also, as by one born out of due time.

faqs.question: What does he say “labored” means?
faqs.answer: He asks “What’s another word for labor? Work.” and says the grace of God was with Paul as he labored.

scriptures.text_nkjv: For I am the least of the apostles, who am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the church of God. But by the grace of God I am what I am, and His grace toward me was not in vain; but I labored more abundantly than they all, yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me. Therefore, whether it was I or they, so we preach and so you believed.

faqs.question: Does he say grace is only something given to us?
faqs.answer: No. He says “it also is a power that moves us.”

faqs.question: How does he describe grace as a divine influence?
faqs.answer: He says it is “the divine influence or power upon the heart,” and the heart is “The mind, the emotions, and the will.”

faqs.question: What does he say grace did for Peter?
faqs.answer: He says “grace moved God to reach out to Peter and bring him back,” even though Peter had denied Him.

scriptures.text_nkjv: But whoever denies Me before men, him I will also deny before My Father who is in heaven.

faqs.question: What does he say about Jesus increasing in grace?
faqs.answer: He says “He increased in grace” with God and men, and that grace moved Him to please the Father and to touch people.

scriptures.text_nkjv: And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favor with God and men.

faqs.question: How does he say grace differs from a favor?
faqs.answer: He says a favor “doesn’t change him,” but “if I influence him to change to a better man, that is what grace is about.”

faqs.question: Does he say grace is a free gift?
faqs.answer: Yes. He says grace “is a free gift, but you got to accept it and use it.”

faqs.question: What does he say grace does for worship?
faqs.answer: He says “Grace wants you to worship God,” and that when His presence comes, “you start taking on His nature.”

scriptures.text_nkjv: Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom, teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord.

faqs.question: Does he say everyone can be a disciple?
faqs.answer: Yes. He says “you may not be an apostle, but you can still be a light to the world. You can be a disciple of Christ.”
